entries.summary: A security and reliability pass over the desktop app, the mod index and the website: shared backup codes can no longer redirect where mods are installed, the app asks Windows for far fewer permissions, and store requests survive a dropped connection.
highlights: Importing a shared profile or backup code can no longer change where mods are installed. Folder settings now always stay the ones chosen on this machine, and a code carrying an odd profile name can no longer point installs outside your mods folder.
The app now asks the operating system for much less: opening a profile folder is one built-in action instead of blanket permission to open any file and create any directory.
Fixed on Windows: the default mods location (%APPDATA%\rsmm\mods) was never expanded, so "Open folder" could create a literal "%APPDATA%" folder beside the app instead of opening the real one.

Store and index requests now retry briefly through a dropped connection or a temporary server hiccup instead of failing straight to an error. Uploads and edits are never retried, so nothing is submitted twice.
Website: mod, guide and collection pages no longer render publisher-supplied links or text into the page unchecked. Links must be ordinary http(s) addresses, and page metadata is escaped.
Fixed: "What's new" could fold several loader-only updates into a single entry, hiding notes you had not seen yet.

entries.summary: Mod failures are now durable and visible: a mod whose init.lua fails is recorded in the health file and reported by rsmm doctor, repeated handler errors latch instead of flooding the log, and one failing hook installer no longer stops every other capability from arming.
highlights: A mod whose init.lua fails is now recorded in the health file and reported by rsmm doctor, instead of vanishing into a log that rotates away.
Repeated handler errors latch after a few consecutive failures rather than writing a line per event fire.
One failing hook installer no longer stops every other capability from arming, or blocks mods from starting.
A mod that raises a non-string error (error{...}) no longer takes the game down from inside the loader's own error handler; Lua errors now carry a full traceback.

entries.summary: Uninstalling a mod now runs its cleanup step, so a mod can no longer leave game settings behind after it is gone.
highlights: Mods can ship a cleanup step that undoes settings they changed while running. In the installed app that step never actually ran — it only worked in a development checkout — so every mod's cleanup had been silently doing nothing. It runs now.

Uninstalling a mod deleted its folder before giving it a chance to clean up, which removed the only thing that knew how to undo the change. Reported as a run seed that stayed frozen after a seed-pinning mod was removed: the mod was gone, its setting was not. Cleanup now runs first.
If a mod's cleanup cannot run — it failed, or the mod folder was deleted by hand while it was still enabled — the app says so instead of reporting a clean uninstall that quietly left settings behind.
Publishing a mod from the app wrote the packaged file into a temporary folder that was deleted a moment later, so the upload had nothing to send. It now writes somewhere that lasts.

entries.summary: Stutter fixes for the damage meter, and it now attributes a transformed hero to the right player.
highlights: Fixed the stuttering reported in co-op. The meter's background probes were asking the operating system about a page of memory once per value read — tens of thousands of times a second. They now read a page at a time, which the game's own thread feels as a stutter no longer competing with it.

An ability that swaps your hero — Sun Wukong's transform, a respawn — no longer counts you as a second player. Your damage follows you through it, and for allies too, using the identity the game itself stamps on every hit.
Hits the game does not count are no longer counted by the meter either, so the board matches the end-of-run screen. Rows now show kills.
Turning the meter off now stops its background work as well as its counting, and a board that has split a player into two rows no longer guesses names.

entries.summary: The game loader now shows a download bar and can restart the game for you, publishing a mod version cannot mislabel it, and restoring no longer deletes the previous run's log.
highlights: Updating the game loader now shows a real download bar instead of a spinner, and offers to restart Ravenswatch when it finishes — a running game keeps the loader it started with, so the update only takes effect in a fresh session. If a run is in progress it asks first.

Fixed installed mods arriving switched off. A mod packaged while its author had it disabled shipped that setting with it, so it installed, applied, and then did nothing — with no error anywhere, because a disabled mod has its code removed rather than skipped. Packaging now always marks the mod as on, and whether you run it stays your choice in the launcher.

Publishing a mod version now checks that the version you are publishing matches the one inside the package. When they disagreed, the store offered an update that installed correctly and never changed the version, so pressing Update appeared to do nothing forever.

Restoring no longer deletes the previous run's log. The loader archives it at the start of the next launch, and restore was removing it first — so the archive it was supposed to produce never had anything to save, and neither did the crash history that decides whether a mod is disabled after repeated failed launches.
The launcher now tells you when the loader planted in your game folder is not the one it carries, instead of reporting everything as up to date.

entries.summary: Release notes now update on their own, the store gained filters and a list view, and the damage meter stops lagging co-op runs.
highlights: Release notes ship on their own channel, so a loader or scripting fix can announce itself without waiting for a launcher build. What's new appears once after an update, and lives in Settings under About.

Fixed the damage meter lagging co-op runs. A player whose name is not plain ASCII, such as 7♣, read back as nameless, and that left two identity searches running for the whole match instead of stopping once every row was named.
The damage meter now lists everyone in the lobby, including players who have not dealt damage yet. A support who spends the opening minutes healing was previously missing from the board entirely.

The store has filters for category, tag and rating, a switch to hide mods you already have, and a dense list view beside the existing cards. Picking a mod in the list opens its page next to the results.
Settings gained an About tab and moved to the foot of the sidebar, which now collapses to icons.
Interface animations can be turned off in Settings, and the hover movement is gone.
The launcher and game loader versions are shown in the corner of the window.

entries.summary: Damage-meter ally names, and the loader version is now visible in Settings.
highlights: Ally rows in the damage meter are named from the netcode peer table instead of a positional guess, so names stay correct in co-op.
Settings shows the running launcher version alongside the planted game-loader version, with pending updates for each.
Refreshed the function-pattern database against the 2026-08-20 game build.

entries.summary: Damage-meter accuracy and a banner for loader-channel updates.
highlights: The damage board no longer counts destructible props as combatants.
The identity scan that could stall the game during a run has been retired.
Loader and Lua SDK updates now announce themselves in-app, including when Ravenswatch is holding the loader open and needs closing first.

entries.summary: The game loader and Lua SDK now update without a launcher release.
highlights: A signed rolling update channel ships the loader DLL and Lua SDK straight into the game directory, so a scripting fix no longer waits on a full launcher release and reinstall.
Every payload is verified against the same signing key as the launcher itself, with a fixed destination allowlist. There is no unsigned path.
RSMM_GAME_DIR is honoured everywhere the game directory is resolved.
